public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Primes and perfect squares

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%27s_problems#Near-square_primes)
-/

@[expose] public section


namespace PrimesAndPerfectSquares

/--
Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p - 1$ is a perfect square? In other words: Are there infinitely many primes of the form $n^2 + 1$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_prime_sq_add_one :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {n : ℕ | Prime (n^2 + 1)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end PrimesAndPerfectSquares

reformulations.difference: Lean asks for infinitely many natural-number inputs n with Prime (n^2 + 1), whereas Wikipedia asks for infinitely many prime values p with p - 1 a perfect square, equivalently p = n^2 + 1 for an integer n.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The map n ↦ n^2 + 1 is injective on ℕ, so its image is infinite exactly when the qualifying input set is infinite. Its image consists precisely of primes p with p - 1 a square. Allowing integer roots gives the same prime values, since replacing an integer root by its natural absolute value preserves its square. Mathlib's Prime on ℕ agrees with Nat.Prime. Both infinitude equivalences were proved in /workspace/review/scratch.lean without using the conjecture or sorry.

review.notes: Checked the sole declaration, answer scope and polarity, underlying definitions, and small inputs n = 0 through 15. At n = 0 the value is 1, which is not prime, so no positivity restriction is missing. Wikipedia records all four Landau problems as unresolved as of 2026, consistent with the research open tag. The scratch file compiles successfully; the equivalence proofs have no sorryAx dependencies.
